text: One platform-owned store holds feature_flag and feature_flag_change, with the schema name allocated by RWB-PLT-DB, the library caches the flag values per service, and the admin component deploys with the rwb-integration platform route.
why: The flags belong to the platform library by default ruling, so the two tables exist once and not once per service; no source names the store, its schema or the deployment, and the story cannot build without one of each.
read: Template and Rules section R3 default ruling (feature flags to the platform library); Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 20 (every service from the service template and shared libraries) and slide 29 (one schema and login per service); Ownership Map ruling on feature_flag
confirm: Platform team and ACE DBA at the wave 0 design gate
impact: Names the store, the per-service cache and the deployment only; no business value changes

text: The four feature-flag paths stay exactly as the Ownership Map names them (GET /feature-flags, GET /admin/feature-flags, POST /admin/feature-flags, PATCH /admin/feature-flags/{flagKey}), at v1 and with no service segment, because the platform library has no service short.
why: Template and Rules section R4 gives every service a REST base under its short; the platform library has none and the Ownership Map fixes the four paths without a segment, so adding a segment would invent a service name and break every consumer.
read: Ownership Map v1 api entries GET /feature-flags, GET /admin/feature-flags, POST /admin/feature-flags and PATCH /admin/feature-flags/{flagKey}; Template and Rules section R4
applied_in: RWB-PLT-E1047-APP sections 3 and 12.1; RWB-PLT-E1047-CON sections 1 and 12.1
confirm: API review at the contract freeze
impact: The four published paths; no service short is invented and no path changes

text: The 30-second cache interval of the legacy story stays the default interval of the library and is held as a chart value, never as a code constant.
why: The legacy story already marks the value assumed (DL11), and the realignment holds tunables as chart values, so the same number stays the default while a deployment can change it without a build.
read: Legacy RWB-E1-047 section 4 step 3 and section 13 (property rwb.flags.cache-seconds = 30, assumed; DL11)
confirm: Platform team at the performance test of the library
impact: The latency of a flag change in every service; no business rule changes

text: The published feature-flag schemas carry the legacy field identifiers DF-OPS-207 to DF-OPS-223 and the standard columns created_by and created_at, and the schema names of the two tables stay as the placeholder until RWB-PLT-DB allocates them.
why: No technical specification exists for the platform library and no source names the table schemas; the legacy field identifiers are the only defined column set, so they are published rather than invented.
read: Legacy RWB-E1-047 section 11 (Data table); Logical Data Model and Data Dictionary field identifiers
confirm: Contract freeze with the platform team and the ACE DBA
impact: The fields and schema names of the published documents; no business value changes

text: POST /admin/feature-flags carries an Idempotency-Key and answers 409 for a duplicate key, while PATCH /admin/feature-flags/{flagKey} is guarded by If-Match with the version instead of an Idempotency-Key.
why: Architecture v5 slide 11 requires an Idempotency-Key on every POST and RFC 9457 problem details, and the legacy contract states uniqueness on the POST and a version check on the PATCH without naming a header; the higher source wins and the loser is recorded.
read: Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 11 (Idempotency-Key on every POST; RFC 9457 problem details); legacy RWB-E1-047 section 12 contract rows
confirm: API review at the contract freeze
impact: Adds one header to the POST and keeps If-Match on the PATCH; the four operations and the four paths are unchanged

text: The rule-model fetch returns one response carrying the package code, the package version label, the checksum, the ordered rows of that version and the catalog projection of each row (action text, owner role, timer spec and outputs); every service that embeds the kit subscribes to RulePackageInForce on rwb.decision.events.v1 through its own inbox.
why: Architecture v5 slides 14 and 27 and Temporal and Drools design slide 15 name GET /rule-models/{n}/{v} and the checksum-verify-and-swap step, but no source gives the response shape, an Ownership Map row for the path, or a subscriber list beyond the four services on slide 43.
read: The kit's model loader and its contract fake are written to one response object with packageCode, packageVersion, checksum, rows[] and, per row, action_text, owner_role, timer_spec and outputs; the catalog answer therefore needs no second call and no read of rule_row. Subscriptions follow DP-04 rather than the partial consumer list of slide 43.
applied_in: RWB-PLT-E1072-APP sections 11, 12.2, 12.4 and 13; RWB-PLT-E1072-CON sections 7 and 12
confirm: The rwb-decision owner and the platform contract owner at the contract freeze
impact: If the payload differs, the model loader, the contract schema and the kit fake change; neither the four published interfaces nor the refusal change.

text: The phase-1 package format stays the XLS decision table compiled to DRL, which is what the governance story uploads and what the model fetch delivers; OMG DMN 1.6 is the later target on the same Drools runtime and no date is set for it.
why: Architecture v5 slide 27 and Temporal and Drools design slide 15 describe the XLS-to-DRL path and the DMN 1.6 migration as a proposal without a date, and the legacy story builds on the XLS tables and the generated DRL.
read: The kit compiles the DRL of the fetched version; it declares no DMN parser and no format switch in phase 1, and a later DMN model arrives through the same fetch and the same interfaces.
confirm: The rwb-decision owner when the DMN migration is scheduled
impact: If DMN arrives in phase 1, the loader gains a format discriminator in the model payload; the interfaces and the refusal stay as they are.

text: The cache maximum 20 from the legacy story stays the default of the kit and is read at run time through the parameters contract as drools.kiebase.cache.max; it is never a code constant and no other bound is introduced.
why: The legacy story fixed the parameter at 20 through the parameters catalog (section 3 and section 13) and DP-06 moves parameters to the rwb-case contract, but no source restates the value or says what happens when the read fails.
read: The kit reads the bound from GET /api/recovery/case/v1/admin/parameters, falls back to the documented default 20 when the catalog holds no value or the read fails, raises an alert in that case and keeps the last known bound in memory.
applied_in: RWB-PLT-E1072-APP sections 3, 5, 12.2 and 13; RWB-PLT-E1072-CON sections 7, 12.2 and 17
confirm: The rwb-case parameters owner and the platform library owner
impact: If the catalog carries another value, only the configuration changes; a code constant would be a defect under the guardrails of both stories.

text: The kit keeps the legacy interface shapes and the Java package of the legacy story, is published as one versioned library artefact per platform release, and its artefact coordinates and the error codes of a refused model fetch are taken from the platform library baseline and from the rwb-decision contract rather than fixed here.
why: No source states the group, the artefact name or the release cadence of the embedded kit, and no source gives the HTTP status codes, the problem type or the message catalogue of a refused or failed model fetch on rwb-decision.
read: The contract publishes the four interfaces and the refusal of the kit's own exception, leaves the artefact coordinates as the platform baseline's, and leaves the transport errors of the fetch to the rwb-decision document when it is published; a consumer pins the kit version and not a coordinate it invents.
confirm: The platform library owner and the rwb-decision owner at the contract freeze
impact: If the baseline names the artefact differently, only the publication coordinates change; if rwb-decision publishes its own fetch errors, section 14 gains a pass-through row and no interface changes.

text: The refusal keeps the message identifier MSG-P3-027 with the legacy text and stays non-retryable, even though the store, the governance and the refusal now sit with rwb-decision (P7); no renumbering is done in this run.
why: The legacy story carries MSG-P3-027 for both the no-version-in-force path and the checksum path (sections 5 and 14), Temporal and Drools design slide 28 makes a missing version a stop with no retry, and no source publishes a message catalogue for rwb-decision that would replace the identifier.
read: NoPackageInForce carries messageId MSG-P3-027 and the package code; the activity failure is non-retryable; the text stays 'The rule version was refused at the {check} check: {detail}.' with {check} naming checksum or package in force and {detail} naming the package code and the version label only.
applied_in: RWB-PLT-E1072-APP sections 5, 8, 13 and 14; RWB-PLT-E1072-CON sections 7, 8 and 14
confirm: The rwb-decision owner and the message catalogue owner
impact: A renumbered identifier would change the refusal in the contract, the kit exception and every decision record that cites the check; nothing else in either story changes.

text: The retry ladder is the Kafka retry topics at 1 min, 10 min and 1 h after the failed attempt and then the dead-letter topic with one alert and the replay tool, as Architecture v5 slides 11 and 22 fix it; the legacy 3 retries at 1, 5 and 15 minutes stay only in the copied criteria text and are exercised through the retry-window configuration of the library, so a test proves the windows come from configuration and not from code.
why: The legacy story and the architecture disagree on the retry schedule. Under R-PREC (Template and Rules section R3) the Arch v5 catalogue slides outrank the story master, so the Kafka ladder wins, but the legacy criteria are copied unchanged and must still be repeatable through configuration.
read: Legacy RWB-TE-006 sections 3, 4, 5 and 12; Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slides 11, 22 and 34; Recovery Workbench Temporal and Drools Design Text Extract v1 slide 28
impact: The retry topics and the windows appear in the relay configuration and in the test fixtures; a change is a configuration change with no code change, because the windows are parameters and not constants.

text: The legacy Quartz job JOB-11 Outbox sender becomes a continuous per-service outbox relay inside each service, started with the service and driven by a poll of the due rows with a skip-locked selection, and it is not a Temporal Schedule and not a shared Quartz table; the legacy assumed batch size of 200 per run is kept as a configurable batch size per poll, and every service runs at least one relay instance so that Kafka being down leaves the rows in its own outbox. Each service's own database story applies its copy of the four tables in its own schema.
why: Architecture v5 slide 44 gives JOB-11 the owner every service with the mechanism outbox relay to Kafka, slide 20 gives every service a continuous outbox relay, and the Ownership Map records JOB-11 with the replacement no Temporal Schedule, outbox relay to Kafka in every service. The exact poll interval, the batch size and the number of relay instances are not stated.
read: Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slides 20, 22, 34 and 44; Ownership Map jobs JOB-11; Legacy RWB-TE-006 section 13 configuration and build step 7
impact: The service template gains one relay bean but no Schedule, no Temporal workflow and no shared job table; the poll interval and the batch size are parameters, and a change does not touch the data model.

text: The library owns the store, the relay, the retry climb and the dead-letter path of a delivery, and it raises one alert to the platform administrator for a record that reaches the dead-letter topic; the case-step effects stay in the code of the service that owns the case step, which raises SYSTEM_UNAVAILABLE, RETRY_SUCCEEDED and RETRY_LIMIT_REACHED, raises the task RESOLVE_OUTBOX_DELIVERY for the recipient owner role and writes its own decision-record entry in its own transaction, so the library raises no case event, no task and no decision record of its own.
why: The legacy story performs all of it inside one module, but in the target a shared library cannot write another service's case state or decision record; the architecture puts the case events, the tasks and the decision record with the owning service (R-UNI-33, R-UNI-35, R-UNI-36, R-UNI-39) and the retry and dead-letter path with Kafka and the platform team. No source states the split explicitly for the library.
read: Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slides 11, 14, 22, 28 and 44; Recovery Workbench Temporal and Drools Design Text Extract v1 slides 13, 14 and 28; Legacy RWB-TE-006 sections 4, 5 and 12
confirm: Platform team and the case-step owner services
impact: Each consuming service keeps a small case-step handler and a decision-record call; the library exposes the failure to the caller instead of acting on the case, so a change of the case-step contract does not change the library.

text: The library contract is one published artifact with major version 1, its interfaces, its DDL template and its fakes, published on the platform library channel of the service template and consumed by every service as a pinned version; the retry ladder that the contract refers to is the Kafka retry topics at 1 min, 10 min and 1 h and then the dead-letter topic, while the legacy 3 retries at 1, 5 and 15 minutes stay only in the copied criteria text of the APP story and are exercised through configuration. The column set of processed_event and idempotency_key is the working read of that template until a field list is published; outbox_event and outbox_delivery keep the legacy fields DF-OPS-189 to DF-OPS-206.
why: The legacy story publishes the interfaces inside one module and fixes the retry schedule as configuration with different values from the architecture; the target needs one pinned artifact per service and a single ladder, and no source gives the artifact name, the version scheme or the publication channel.
read: Legacy RWB-TE-006 section 12; Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slides 11, 20, 22 and 29; Template and Rules v1 sections R3 and R5.5 (DP-09)
impact: A version change reaches every service through its pinned dependency and its contract test; the retry windows are configuration, so the ladder change needs no interface change.

text: The contract states that the legacy Quartz JOB-11 sender becomes a continuous per-service outbox relay driven by the service lifecycle, that no Temporal Schedule and no shared Quartz table replaces it, and that the relay is the only publisher of the caller's records to the owning service topic rwb.<short>.events.v1 with the CloudEvents 1.0 envelope, the caseId record key and an idempotent producer with acks=all.
why: Architecture v5 slides 20 and 44 give every service a continuous outbox relay and record JOB-11 with no Temporal Schedule, but no source says whether the relay is a workflow, a worker or a Schedule, and the contract must fix it before the services build.
read: Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slides 11, 20, 22 and 44; Ownership Map jobs JOB-11
impact: Every service builds one relay component from the template and no Schedule; a change of the poll interval or the batch size is a configuration change.

text: The contract states that the case-step events, the task RESOLVE_OUTBOX_DELIVERY for the recipient owner role and the decision-record entry belong to the service that owns the case step and are reached through that service's published contract, and that the library raises no case event, no task and no decision record of its own; the library reports the failure to its caller and raises one alert to the platform administrator on the dead-letter path.
why: The legacy story raises the task, the case event and the decision record in the same transaction as the move, which one shared library cannot do in a 19-service split; the architecture keeps the case state, the tasks and the decision record with the owning service, but no source states the split for the library.
read: Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slides 14, 22, 28, 41 and 42; Recovery Workbench Temporal and Drools Design Text Extract v1 slides 13, 14 and 28; Legacy RWB-TE-006 sections 4, 5 and 12
confirm: Platform team and the case-step owner services
impact: The contract test proves the library raises nothing on the case; a change of the case-step contract touches the owning service only and not the library.

text: The platform package registry publishes the baseline as one versioned set of packages, each with its source, software bill of materials, checksum, changelog entry and usage example, and the service template pins exactly one version of that set, so a service never chooses a library version of its own.
why: No source read gives the registry, the coordinates, the module list or the baseline version, and the story cannot be tested without a delivery shape and a pin.
read: Architecture v5 slides 20, 38 and 49; legacy NF-02 description (publish to the package registry with versioning and usage examples); Template and Rules v1 section R9 placeholder rule.
applied_in: Section 1, section 3 Preconditions, section 4 Flow, section 7 Acceptance criteria AC1 and AC2, section 13 Solution plan and section 14 Validation and messages
impact: The release, the pin and the drift gate can be built and tested; a different registry, module split or version changes coordinates, file paths and the release note only, not the acceptance criteria.

text: The baseline covers exactly the five areas the legacy description lists - logging and tracing, authentication and authorisation, RBAC, error handling and configuration - and nothing else is added to the baseline set at wave 0.
why: The legacy key is a one-sentence delivery statement and no source enumerates the modules further, so the story must fix a scope for the release and the examples.
read: Legacy NF-02 description (logging and tracing, authentication and authorisation, RBAC, error handling, configuration); Architecture v5 slides 11, 20, 22 and 35 for the standards each area carries.
applied_in: Section 1, section 7 Acceptance criteria Background, section 8 Business rules, section 11 Data and section 13 Solution plan (module split)
impact: The release is scoped to five areas; a later module is a new baseline version and a new pin, and no existing criterion changes.

text: NF-02 has no runtime surface of its own: the baseline creates no service, schema, topic, queue, workflow, schedule, screen or REST base, and it changes no business behaviour, so every contract table in section 12 is None and the deliverable is a package set plus the template wiring and the usage examples.
why: The key is a Moved (no impact) delivery task for shared libraries, while the realignment forbids inventing a service short name, schema, topic, queue or REST base for a platform library that is not one of the 19 services.
read: Template and Rules v1 section R4 (19 services, each with a short name) and section R5.1 (RWB-PLT-LIB is a platform epic); Change Register v1 NF-02 row (Moved (no impact)); Architecture v5 slide 20 (every service comes from the template and the shared libraries).
applied_in: Section 1, section 8 Business rules BR8, section 12 Contract (12.7 and 12.9), section 13 Solution plan and section 19 Out of scope
impact: No schema, topic, queue or REST base is invented for the platform library and nothing is deployed by this story; a later platform runtime surface is a separate story, not a change to this one.
